newsitem.title: USA: State, local officials press Gore on air standards.
newsitem.headline: State, local officials press Gore on air standards.

text.p: State and local government officials urged the White House on Friday to take their concerns into account before the administration issues a new rule to tighten air quality standards in July.

In an hour-long meeting with Vice President Al Gore, representatives from seven state and local government associations pressed the administration to pay more attention to their concerns on a range of issues from the costs of meeting new clear air standards to an Internet tax.
New York Gov. George Pataki, a Republican who was the only governor to attend the meeting, said Gore was responsive but made no commitments on policy.
"On none of the issues did he make a promise that he was going to effectuate a particular type of policy," Pataki told reporters after the meeting.

While states were divided over clean air policy, they were all concerned about the costs of meeting more stringent limits proposed by the Environmental Protection Agency for soot or particulates and smog-forming ozone.

Dan Sprague, executive director of the Council of State Governments, said state and local governments were concerned that the proposal violated the unfunded mandates reform act and an order by Clinton that federal agencies should take into consideration cost shifts to states and cities when writing new rules.
"We believe there are huge cost consequences to meeting the new air standards ... and we're not feeling we're included sufficiently in the dialogue on that," said Sprague, who attended the meeting.

Environmentalists pressing for higher standards feared the White House might cave in to heavy pressure from industry and local government groups, who argued that the standards would cost billions of dollars to meet with little health benefit.

Gore has declined to comment publicly on the rule, and green groups who see him as their ally are worried about his silence amid a review by the White House's National Economic Council and its Council on Environmental Quality of the EPA proposal.
"(Gore) indicated that he was sensitive to our concerns but basically the process was going to have to play itself out," Sprague said. "He heard us, but he did not commit to anything."

The White House has been conducting meetings with the EPA and other federal agencies -- many of which have raised objections to the EPA plan -- to decide whether to adopt, change or drop the proposal.

"We are still engaged in an inter-agency process. A decision has not been made, but it will be in the next two weeks," an EPA spokeswoman said. She said the decision could come next week on the rule which under a court order must be made final in July.
